prompt: What does PageSpeed Insights show that a Lighthouse run on your computer does not?

choices.text: A score for accessibility

choices.text: A trace of the main thread

choices.text: The page's source code, with the slow lines marked

choices.text: The planner has no HTML

choices.text: It loads from its machines, which cannot reach yours

choices.text: It needs Firefox

prompt: What does CHROME_PATH tell Lighthouse?

choices.text: The browser to open

choices.text: Which page to measure

choices.text: How slow the network should be

prompt: You open a new terminal and Lighthouse cannot find Chrome. What happened?

choices.text: The server stopped
choices.why: That would give a different error.

choices.text: export is per terminal

prompt: The course page scored 100 and the report still listed three insights. Why is that no contradiction?

choices.text: Insights look past this one load
choices.why: Right: on another page, network or visit.

choices.text: Insights are never counted
choices.why: They inform; the score is the five metrics.

choices.text: The score and the insights were from different runs
choices.why: Both came from one report.

choices.text: A score of 100 is rounded down to 99 for every insight
choices.why: No such rule exists.

prompt: Match each metric to its weight in the performance score.
Why does the score use TBT and not INP?

choices.text: INP is not supported by Chromium
choices.why: Lesson 5 measured it in Chromium.

choices.text: TBT is newer than INP and replaced it
choices.why: They measure different things.

choices.text: Nobody interacts during a load
choices.why: Yes. TBT measures what would make a click wait.

choices.text: INP is only for desktops
choices.why: It applies to every device.

prompt: During a load, one task of 120 ms and one of 40 ms ran after the first paint. How much TBT do they add, in milliseconds?
hint: Only the part of each long task past 50 ms.

prompt: A page scores 100 in Lighthouse. Can it still fail the Core Web Vitals?

choices.text: No, a 100 means every metric is good
choices.why: Only for that one load.

choices.text: Yes: the assessment is field data
choices.why: Right. Real visitors click things Lighthouse never clicks.

choices.text: Only on desktop
choices.why: Phones and desktops are judged apart, either can fail.

choices.text: No, because Lighthouse already uses the 75th percentile
choices.why: A Lighthouse run is one load, with no percentile.

prompt: The heavy home page shows a hundred courses. Why was its first response over 600 KB?

choices.text: It lists all five thousand courses as links
choices.why: Since lesson 5 it lists a hundred.

choices.text: The script is inlined
choices.why: The script is a separate file.

choices.text: Lighthouse added its own code to the page
choices.why: curl measured the same size.

choices.text: It embeds the whole plan, uncompressed
choices.why: Yes: lesson 4's hydration data, sent as it is.

prompt: Why did gzip make the page about twelve times smaller?

choices.text: The text repeats itself a lot
choices.why: Right: names like course-4182, thousands of times.

choices.text: It removes the parts nobody reads
choices.why: It keeps every byte; the browser gets them all back.

choices.text: curl drops the JSON
choices.why: curl passed it all to gzip.

choices.text: It converts the HTML into a binary format that browsers read faster
choices.why: It is the same HTML once uncompressed.

prompt: Which insight named the cause of the heavy page?

choices.text: Render-blocking requests
choices.why: That one is about the stylesheet.

choices.text: Use efficient cache lifetimes
choices.why: That one is about repeat visits.

choices.text: Document request latency
choices.why: Yes: no compression applied, on the first request.

choices.text: Network dependency tree
choices.why: That one is about chains of requests.

prompt: What does Lighthouse's default throttling method, simulate, do?

choices.text: Slows the browser down for real
choices.why: That is devtools.

choices.text: Loads at full speed and computes the slow load
choices.why: Right, with a model of the network and the processor.

choices.text: Uses field data from CrUX
choices.why: Lighthouse is lab data.

choices.text: Loads the page on a real phone
choices.why: It pretends to be one.

prompt: On the heavy page, the slowed browser painted at about 1.3 s and the model said 4.3 s. Why?

choices.text: devtools throttling is disabled on localhost
choices.why: The HTML took four seconds; it was slowed.

choices.text: The first run warmed a cache
choices.why: Every run disagreed the same way.

choices.text: The model counts the favicon
choices.why: The favicon is not the paint.

choices.text: The model waits for the whole document
choices.why: Yes, and the browser drew the top before the plan arrived.

prompt: If the page painted after about one second, what did the four seconds still cost?

choices.text: The module script ran only then
choices.why: Right: three seconds of looking ready without working.

choices.text: Nothing; the model was simply wrong
choices.why: The paint was early; the script was not.

choices.text: A layout shift
choices.why: CLS was zero.

choices.text: The stylesheet arrived late
choices.why: It arrived at about 1.2 s.

prompt: Which habits make a before-and-after with Lighthouse trustworthy? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: One throttling method for both
choices.why: Yes: the two methods measure different things.

choices.text: Several runs, keeping the median
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Reading what a surprising number is made of
choices.why: Yes, as the requests showed here.

choices.text: Keeping the best run of each
choices.why: The best run flatters both.

choices.text: Switching to desktop for the after
choices.why: That changes the conditions, not the page.

prompt: How does the server know it may send gzip?

choices.text: Every browser reads gzip, so it never checks
choices.why: send checks the header on every request.

choices.text: From the file's extension
choices.why: Extensions set the type, not the encoding.

choices.text: The browser's accept-encoding header says so
choices.why: Right. The answer says content-encoding: gzip.

choices.text: From a cookie
choices.why: No cookie is involved.

prompt: Why does send also write vary: accept-encoding?

choices.text: Browsers refuse gzip without it
choices.why: They read content-encoding.

choices.text: So a cache keeps one copy per encoding
choices.why: Yes. Otherwise it could hand gzip to a client that cannot read it.

choices.text: It makes the response smaller
choices.why: It adds a header.

choices.text: Lighthouse insists on it before it scores
choices.why: The score went up for the compression.

prompt: In production, where is compression usually done?

choices.text: In the browser, before the request
choices.why: The browser decompresses answers.

choices.text: In the database
choices.why: The database sends data, not responses.

choices.text: In the build, for every page drawn per request
choices.why: A page drawn per request does not exist at build time.

choices.text: In a reverse proxy or the CDN
choices.why: Right. Check a real response before adding it to the app.

prompt: What is an estimated saving in a Lighthouse insight?

choices.text: The time the fix will save every visitor
choices.why: It is not a promise.

choices.text: The points the score will rise by
choices.why: It is in milliseconds or kilobytes.

choices.text: A figure taken from CrUX
choices.why: It comes from the lab run.

choices.why: Those are side by side.

choices.text: A server error
choices.why: Errors are not a shape.
